questions.text: What is known as the combination of high inflation, high unemployment and stagnant growth?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is option (2) i.e Stagflation

  • It is a phenomenon wherein the inflation rate and the unemployment rate is high and the economic growth rate slows down.
  • Stagflation = High Inflation + High Unemployment + Stagnant Growth.
  • It raises a dilemma for economic policy since actions designed to lower inflation may increase unemployment and vice versa.
  • It is unusual because policies to reduce inflation make life difficult for the unemployed, while steps to alleviate unemployment increase inflation.
  • Stagflation led to the emergence of the Misery index.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT one of the fiscal measures to contain inflation?

options.text: Removing levy obligations in case of sugar
Decreasing the stock limit of some commodities

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is option (5) i.e Decreasing the stock limit of some commodities

  • The government has taken a number of measures to contain inflation. The measures include reducing Import Duties, allowing imports of the commodities which are scarce in the market, and removing levy obligations in case of sugar.
  • It also includes banning exports of commodities such as rice and oils and imposing minimum export prices.
  • It also contains suspending or banning the futures trading is come commodities and raising the stock limit of some commodities.
  • It is necessary to make available commodities via various organizations such as NAFED and NCCF.
  • National Agricultural Cooperative Marketing Federation of India Ltd. (NAFED)
  • The National Cooperative Consumers' Federation of India Ltd. (NCCF)

questions.text: Which one of the following is a measure of general price inflation?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is option (1) i.e GDP Deflator

  • GDP Deflator is an indicator of general price inflation. It is calculated by dividing nominal GDP by real GDP and then multiplying by 100.
  • Nominal GDP is the market value of goods and services produced in an economy, not adjusted for inflation. 
    (measured at current prices). 
  • Real GDP is nominal GDP, adjusted for inflation to reflect changes in real output (measured at constant prices).  
  • GDP Deflator = (GDP at Current Prices/GDP at constant Price) * 100.
  • GDP deflator reflects the prices of all domestically produced goods and services in the economy whereas, other measures like CPI and WPI are based on a fixed basket of goods and services, thereby not representing the entire economy.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT the probable effects of the inflation?

options.text: Inflation encourages current consumption and discourages savings
The real rate of interest is reduced in times of inflation
High levels of inflation reduce confidence and increase uncertainty
High rate of inflation will hit hard the export industry in the economy
Higher inflation is due to decrease in money supply in the economy

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is option (5) i.e Higher inflation is due to a decrease in money supply in the economy

  • Inflation increases current consumption (buy goods and services now before prices rise) and discourages savings. People with savings suffer in times of inflation as the purchasing power of their savings decreases as price levels rise.
  • The real rate of interest (nominal rate less the inflation rate) is reduced in times of inflation. Real interest rates may be negative if the inflation rate is greater than the interest rate.
  • High levels of inflation reduce confidence and increase uncertainty (difficult to predict the future).
  • Inflation can affect business planning. Budgeting becomes difficult because of the uncertainty created by rising inflation which may reduce planned investment spending.
  • A high rate of inflation will hamper the export industry in the economy. The cost of production will increase and the exports will become less competitive in the international market.

questions.text:
Which of the following comes under different types of inflation?

  1. Cost-push Inflation
  2. Demand-pull Inflation
  3. Built-in Inflation
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is option (4) i.e All of these

  • Demand-pull inflation is caused by increases in aggregate demand due to increased private and government spending, etc.
  • The demand-pull theory follows that the rate of inflation accelerates whenever aggregate demand is increased beyond the ability of the economy to produce (its potential output). 
  • Cost-push inflation is caused by a fall in aggregate supply which may be due to natural disasters, or increased prices of inputs. 
  • Producers for whom oil is a part of their costs could then pass this on to consumers in the form of increased prices.
  • Built-in inflation is motivated by adaptive expectations, and is often linked to the “price/wage spiral”. It involves workers trying to keep their wages high with prices (above the rate of inflation), and firms passing these higher labor costs on to their customers as higher prices.

questions.text: Which sector of Indian economy provides highest employment?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Primary.

  • In the Primary sector of the economy, activities are undertaken by directly using natural resources. Agriculture, Mining, Fishing, Forestry, Dairy, etc. are some examples of this sector. It is called so because it forms the base for all other products. Since most of the natural products we get are from agriculture, dairy, forestry, fishing, it is also called Agriculture and the allied sector.
  • Secondary: It includes the industries where finished products are made from natural materials produced in the primary sector. Industrial production, cotton fabric, sugar cane production etc. activities come under this sector.
  • Tertiary: This sector’s activities help in the development of the primary and secondary sectors. By itself, economic activities in the tertiary sector do not produce a goods but they are an aid or support for the production.
  • Quaternary Activities: these are specialized tertiary activities in the ‘Knowledge Sector’ which demands a separate classification. The quaternary sector is the intellectual aspect of the economy. It is the process which enables entrepreneurs to innovate and improve the quality of services offered in the economy.

questions.text: Which indicator is used for analyzing the employment situation in the country?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Worker-Population ratio.

  • The employment-to-population ratio is defined as the proportion of an economy’s working-age population that is employed. As an indicator, the employment-to-population ratio provides information on the ability of an economy to create jobs.
  • Worker Population Ratio is an indicator used for analyzing the employment situation in the country. This is also useful in knowing the proportion of population that is actively contributing to the production of goods and services in the economy.
  • The employment-to-population ratio, also known as the “employment-population ratio,” is a macroeconomic statistic that measures the civilian labor force currently employed against the total working-age population of a region, municipality, or country. It is calculated by dividing the number of people employed by the total number of people of working age, and it is used as a metric of labor and unemployment.
  • Compared with other measures of labor force participation, the employment-to-population ratio is not as affected by seasonal variations or short-term fluctuations in the labor market. As a result, it is often considered to be a more reliable indicator of job shrinkage or growth than the unemployment rate.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT true with respect to Chronic Inflation?

options.text: When Creeping inflation continues for long time it is chronic inflation
It is also known as Secular inflation
It can either be continuous or intermittent
Longer periods of chronic inflation leads to Hyperinflation
Continuous Chronic inflation occurs at regular intervals

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is option (5) i.e Continuous Chronic inflation occurs at regular intervals

  • If creeping inflation persist (continues to increase) for a longer period of time then it is often called Chronic Inflation.
  • It is also known as Secular Inflation.
  • Chronic Creeping Inflation can be Continuous (which remains consistent without any downward movement)
  • It can also be Intermittent (which occurs at regular intervals).
  • It is called chronic because if an inflation rate continues to grow for a longer period without any downturn, then it possibly leads to Hyperinflation.

questions.text:
Which of the following statements is/are true with respect to Headline inflation?

  1. It reflects the prices of all tradeable within an economy.
  2. It contains items such as food and energy.
  3. It does not present an accurate picture of the economy.
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is option (4) i.e All of these

  • Headline inflation reflects the prices of all the tradeable goods within an economy.
  • It includes those items that experience sudden inflationary hikes such as food or energy.
  • Since headline inflation includes everything, it may not present an accurate picture of the current state of the economy.
  • Headline inflation is a measure of the total inflation within an economy, including items such as food and energy prices, which tend to be much more volatile and prone to inflationary spikes.
  • Headline inflation is the raw inflation figure reported through the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

questions.text: Retail Inflation in India is measured by which of the following indices?
questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Consumer Price Index.

Key Points

  • Retail Inflation:
    • Measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI).
  • RBI primarily factors in retail inflation while making its bi-monthly monetary policy.

Important Points

  • Consumer Price Index
    • It measures price changes from the perspective of a retail buyer. It is released by the National Statistical Office (NSO).
    • The CPI calculates the difference in the price of commodities and services such as food, medical care, education, electronics etc, which Indian consumers buy for use.
    • The CPI has several sub-groups including food and beverages, fuel and light, housing and clothing, bedding and footwear.
    • At present, India has five consumer price indexes (CPIs), three of which are working-class specific. These are:
      • CPI for Industrial Workers (IW).
      • CPI for Agricultural Labourer (AL).
      • CPI for Rural Labourer (RL).
    • These three indexes are compiled by the Labour Bureau in the Ministry of Labour and Employment.
